title: Impact of Covenant Violations on Capital Expenditure

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Regression Discontinuity Design (sharp RDD)

• Treatment assignment (covenant “violation”) switches discretely when the debt-to-asset ratio crosses a fixed cutoff.  
• Key identifying assumptions  
 1. Continuity: in the absence of the covenant, firms’ expected log-capex would vary smoothly with the debt-to-asset ratio at the cutoff.  
 2. No precise manipulation: firms cannot perfectly sort their debt-to-asset ratios around the threshold.  

Under these conditions, the jump in log-capex at the cutoff identifies the causal effect of crossing the covenant threshold.

## 2. R Code
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Impact of covenant violations on capital expenditures (RDD)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Required packages
libs <- c("tidyverse", "rdrobust", "rddensity")
invisible(lapply(libs, require, character.only = TRUE))

# 1. Read data ------------------------------------------------
path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s98_data.csv"
df   <- read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)

# 2. Locate the empirical cutoff -----------------------------
#    The lowest running_var that is classified as treated is
#    the point where treatment status changes.
cutoff <- min(df$running_var[df$treated == 1])

cat("Estimated cutoff (debt-to-asset ratio) :", round(cutoff, 4), "\n\n")

# 3. Main RDD estimate ---------------------------------------
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = df$y,
                    x = df$running_var,
                    c = cutoff,          # threshold
                    kernel = "triangular")  # default local-linear

print(rd_main)

# Extract point estimate (robust bias-corrected)
tau_hat <- rd_main$coef[1]
cat("\nRDD point estimate (log-capex jump at cutoff) :", round(tau_hat, 4), "\n")

# 4. Manipulation / sorting test -----------------------------
dens <- rddensity(X = df$running_var, c = cutoff)
cat("\nMcCrary density test p-value :", round(dens$test$p_jkn, 4), "\n")

# 5. Bandwidth robustness ------------------------------------
#   a) 75% of MSE-optimal bandwidth
bw_low  <- 0.75 * rd_main$bws[1,1]
rd_low  <- rdrobust(df$y, df$running_var, c = cutoff, h = bw_low)

#   b) 125% of MSE-optimal bandwidth
bw_high <- 1.25 * rd_main$bws[1,1]
rd_high <- rdrobust(df$y, df$running_var, c = cutoff, h = bw_high)

cat("\nBandwidth-sensitivity (tau hats):",
    "\n  0.75*h  :", round(rd_low$coef[1],  4),
    "\n  1.00*h  :", round(rd_main$coef[1], 4),
    "\n  1.25*h  :", round(rd_high$coef[1], 4), "\n")

# 6. Placebo cutoff ------------------------------------------
placebo_c <- cutoff + 0.20         # arbitrary nearby point
rd_place  <- rdrobust(df$y, df$running_var, c = placebo_c)
cat("\nPlacebo cutoff estimate :", round(rd_place$coef[1], 4),
    "  (should be ~0 if design is valid)\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Economic intuition and prior literature (e.g., Chava & Roberts 2008) suggest that breaching financial covenants tightens lender control and reduces firms’ discretionary spending. Therefore:

• Sign: the jump in log-capex at the cutoff should be negative.  
• Magnitude: around −0.05 to −0.10 log points (≈ 5–10 % reduction in capex) for firms just above versus just below the threshold.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Exploit the discontinuity at the covenant threshold to identify causal effects.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Crossing the covenant threshold leads to a significant increase in capital expenditure.
